title: Confident and wrong
objectives: Explain why a model that predicts likely text can state false facts fluently.

screens.prose: A chatbot is asked for a book and a statistic. The reply is fluent and sure. This reply is an invented example.

lines: You: Recommend a book on market crashes, with one statistic from it.
Chatbot: Read "Ledgers in the Storm: A Short History of Market Panics" (2011).
Chatbot: It shows that 73% of market crashes follow a rise in interest rates.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: The title and the 73% both read smoothly. What can you tell from the reply alone?

options.text: Nothing about whether they are real: fluent text is what it makes
They are real, since it gives a year, a title and a figure
options.why: Details are cheap to write. A year and a percentage make text look checked, but they are just likely tokens.

options.text: They are false, because chatbots make up every book they name
options.why: Often the details are right. You cannot tell which from the text, so you check.

options.text: The book is real, but the 73% may well be made up
options.why: You trusted the title because it is long and specific. That tells you nothing either.

hints.text: Would an invented title read any differently from a real one?
Look at how sure the last line sounds.
The model writes likely text. A real title and an invented one read the same.

feedback.correct: From the text alone you cannot tell. Fluent and sure is how it writes, true or not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the wording alone could tell real from invented.

explain.text: We made up the book and the statistic for this lesson, yet they read as well as real ones. A model writes likely text, so fluency tells you nothing about truth. The rest of this lesson shows why.

screens.prose: Back to the table from ai-basics. The text says "the dog sat on the cat", never "the dog sat on the mat". Step through the sentence one pair at a time.

steps.caption: "dog" after "the": 1 of 6 times in the text, so chance $\tfrac16$.
"sat" after "dog": 1 of 1 times in the text, so chance 1.
"on" after "sat": 2 of 2 times in the text, so chance 1.
"the" after "on": 2 of 2 times in the text, so chance 1.
"mat" after "the": 1 of 6 times in the text, so chance $\tfrac16$.
"." after "mat": 1 of 1 times in the text, so chance 1.

screens.question: Multiply the six chances. What is the chance the table writes this sentence after "the"?

hints.text: Step through all six pairs and note each chance.
Two pairs have chance $\tfrac16$; the other four have chance 1.
Multiply: $\tfrac16 \times \tfrac16 = \tfrac{1}{36}$, and the four 1s change nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the chance of each of the six pairs.

byKey.one-sixth: You used one of the two $\tfrac16$ pairs. Mat after the is also $\tfrac16$, so multiply again.
byKey.added-sixths: You added the two $\tfrac16$ chances. One pair follows another, so the chances multiply.
byKey.zero: You took a sentence not in the text to have chance 0. Every pair in it is in the text, so its chance is not 0.

explain.text: Every pair in the sentence appears in the text, so each has a chance above 0. Multiplying gives $\tfrac16 \times \tfrac16 = \tfrac{1}{36}$, about 0.028. So about 1 run in 36 writes a sentence the text never says.

canvas.caption: Six true pairs, one sentence the text never says.

screens.prose: Every pair is true to the text; the sentence is not in it. A fluent statement that nothing the model saw supports, written because it is likely text, is called a **hallucination**.
screens.question: Why can the table still write this sentence?

options.text: It joins likely pairs, and nothing checks the whole sentence
It remembers the sentence from the text it read
options.why: Search the text: it has "the dog sat on the cat". The mat sentence is new.

options.text: There is a bug in the way the table was built
options.why: The table works as built: it joins likely pairs. That is the point.

options.text: It cannot: a sentence not in the text has chance 0
options.why: You found its chance is $\tfrac{1}{36}$, not 0. About 1 run in 36 writes it.

hints.text: Is each pair in the text?
Each pair had a chance above 0.
The table checks pairs, one at a time. Nothing checks the whole sentence against the text.

feedback.correct: It joins likely pairs. Nothing checks the sentence as a whole.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what the table looks at when it picks a word.

explain.text: The table only ever looks at one pair at a time, and every pair is likely. Nothing compares the finished sentence with the text. A chatbot is far larger, but it too writes likely text with nothing checking it.

screens.prose: Back to the book and the 73%. A chatbot can hallucinate for more than one reason.

lines: You: Recommend a book on market crashes, with one statistic from it.
Chatbot: Read "Ledgers in the Storm: A Short History of Market Panics" (2011).
Chatbot: It shows that 73% of market crashes follow a rise in interest rates.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Select all that apply: why might it write an invented book and figure?

options.text: It predicts likely words, not true ones
It was rewarded for sounding helpful, so it gives an answer
It cannot tell what it does not know
It wants to trick you on purpose
options.why: It has no aim to trick anyone. It writes likely text, as l1 to l3 trained it to.

options.text: Its makers put false facts into it
options.why: Nobody needs to put falsehoods in. Likely text can be false all by itself.

hints.text: Recall each stage: pretraining, fine-tuning, feedback.
One reason comes from each stage you met.
Pretraining predicts likely words; feedback rewards sounding helpful; and nothing tells it where its knowledge stops.

feedback.correct: Likely words, a reward for sounding helpful, and no sense of what it does not know.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each stage of training gives one reason.

explain.text: Pretraining makes it predict likely words, not true ones. Fine-tuning and feedback reward a helpful answer over "I do not know", unless the examples taught doubt. And nothing in training tells it where its knowledge stops.

screens.prose: Sort five claims from this reply. "Likely true" means general and widely known; "check first" means a specific number or source; "likely invented" means no one could know it.

lines: You: I want to start saving. Any facts I should know?
Chatbot: Saving a little each month adds up over the years.
Chatbot: If prices rise, a pound buys less in ten years than it does today.
Chatbot: UK prices rose 4% last year.
Chatbot: A 2017 study, "Habits of Savers", found that 41% of savers stop within a year.
Chatbot: Next year the FTSE 100 will rise exactly 9%.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Drag each claim into its bin.

tokens.text: A pound buys less if prices rise
The FTSE 100 will rise 9% next year

hints.text: Which claims hold a specific number or a named source?
The last line is about next year.
Two general claims are likely true; the 4% and the study need checking; nobody can know next year's rise.

feedback.correct: Two general claims, two to check, and one that no one could know.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask of each claim: is it general, specific, or unknowable?

byKey.four: A specific figure for one year is exactly what to check. It may be right or wrong.
byKey.study: A named study with a percentage is a source to find and read before you use it.
byKey.nine: Nobody can know next year's rise, so an exact figure for it is invented.
byKey.save: That saving adds up is general and widely known. It does not depend on one figure.
byKey.prices: That rising prices shrink what a pound buys is general and widely known.

explain.text: General, widely repeated claims are likely true. Specific numbers and named sources may be right or invented, so check them first. A precise figure for next year is invented, because no one can know it.

screens.prose: Another invented reply: "The firm was founded in 1887. I am certain of this." A colleague says: "It said it was certain, so it must be right."

lines: You: When was the firm founded?
Chatbot: The firm was founded in 1887. I am certain of this.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: What does "I am certain of this" tell you?

options.text: Nothing about truth: it is likely text after a confident answer
That the year is right, because the model said it was sure
options.why: You took its words as a measure of its knowledge. "I am certain" is just more likely text.

options.text: That the model checked the year before replying
options.why: Nothing in the reply was checked. It was written one likely token at a time.

options.text: That the year is wrong, as sure answers usually are
options.why: Sure answers are often right too. The words tell you nothing either way.

hints.text: How was the phrase "I am certain" produced?
It is the second sentence of the reply.
Like every other token, it was written because it is likely text there.

feedback.correct: "I am certain" is more likely text, not a measure of truth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how the phrase itself was written.

byKey.said-sure: You took "I am certain" as a sign the year is right. It is more likely text, written the same way as the year, and checks nothing.

explain.text: A sentence saying "I am certain" is written the same way as the year: because it is likely text. It may follow a right year or a wrong one. Only a check against a source tells you which.

screens.prose: Two replies, both "certain". The first is right. The second is wrong: UK coins went decimal in 1971.

lines: You: What currency does the UK use?
Chatbot: The pound sterling. I am certain of this.
params.title: Reply 1 (invented)

lines: You: In which year did UK coins go decimal?
Chatbot: In 1981. I am certain of this.
params.title: Reply 2 (invented)

screens.question: What would have told the right reply from the wrong one?

options.text: Checking each against a reliable source
A careful reading of the tone of each reply
options.why: The tone is the same in both. Tone tells you nothing here.

options.text: The length of each reply
options.why: Both are short. Length tells you nothing about truth.

options.text: Asking it again whether it is sure
options.why: It would most likely say it is sure again. Asking again gives more likely text, not a check.

hints.text: What is different about how the two replies sound?
Both end with the same sentence.
They sound the same, so only a check against a source can tell them apart.

feedback.correct: Only a check against a source separates them. They sound exactly alike.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what differs between the two replies, apart from the facts.

explain.text: A right answer and a wrong one came with the same words of confidence. Tone tells you nothing. Checking against a reliable source does.

screens.prose: The table multiplied true pairs into a sentence the text never says: $\tfrac16 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times \tfrac16 \times 1 = \tfrac{1}{36}$. A chatbot does the same far larger. So treat every specific name, number, quote and reference as unchecked until you check it.
screens.question: Which parts of a chatbot's reply should you treat as unchecked?

options.text: Every specific name, number, quote and reference
Only the parts where it says it is unsure
options.why: Confidence is likely text too. A sure-sounding claim needs checking as much as any.

options.text: Only the numbers, since names and quotes are safe
options.why: Names, quotes and references are invented as easily as numbers.

options.text: None, as long as the chatbot is widely used
options.why: Every chatbot trained this way writes likely text. Being widely used checks nothing.

feedback.correct: Every specific name, number, quote and reference, until checked.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall which details the book example invented.

screens.prose: An analyst asks a chatbot for a figure for a client pitch. They paste the reply straight in. The reply below is an invented example.

lines: You: What is the average yearly return of the FTSE 100 since 1984?
Chatbot: Since 1984 the FTSE 100 has returned an average of 7.2% a year, including dividends.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: What is the problem, and what should come first?

options.text: The figure is unchecked: find it in the index's published data before using it
None at all, since a figure with a decimal place must be carefully worked out
options.why: A decimal place is cheap to write. A likely-looking number with one is easy text to produce.

options.text: The figure must be wrong, so it should be dropped from the pitch entirely
options.why: It may be right. The point is that you do not know until you check.

options.text: Nothing, as long as asking the chatbot again gives the same answer
options.why: Asking the same model again only gives more likely text, not a check. Level 2 shows real checks.

hints.text: Who checked the 7.2%?
The figure is in the second line.
Nobody did. A figure for clients must be found in the source data first.

feedback.correct: The 7.2% is unchecked. Find it in the index's own published data before it goes to a client. Use the same period, with dividends.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask who has checked the figure so far.

explain.text: The 7.2% might be right, a little off, or invented, and the reply reads the same either way. A client sees it as the firm's claim. So it is checked against the published data first, with the same start year and dividends included.

ideas: A model writes likely text. Joining likely pieces can give a fluent sentence nothing supports: a hallucination.
It happens because the model predicts likely words, was rewarded for sounding helpful, and cannot tell what it does not know.
Tone tells you nothing: "I am certain" is likely text. Treat every specific name, number, quote and reference as unchecked until checked.

formula.name: A fluent sentence the text never says
formula.note: Every pair is in the text; the sentence is not.

summary.trap: "It said it was sure, so it is right" is wrong. A sure tone is likely text, not a check.

quiz.question: From the ai-basics table, "the cat sat on the mat ." is in the text and gets chance $\tfrac{1}{36}$ after "the". "The dog sat on the mat ." is not in the text and also gets $\tfrac{1}{36}$. What does this show?

options.text: The chance cannot tell a sentence in the text from one that is not
Both sentences must be in the text
options.why: Search the text: only the cat sentence is there.

options.text: One of the two chances must be a mistake
options.why: Both are right: $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac13 \times 1 \times 1 \times \tfrac16 \times 1$ and $\tfrac16 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times \tfrac16 \times 1$ are each $\tfrac{1}{36}$.

options.text: A sentence in the text always gets a higher chance
options.why: Here they are equal, so being in the text did not raise the chance.

feedback.correct: Seen and unseen sentences can get the same chance: likely is not the same as true.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two chances.

explain.text: The cat sentence is $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac13 \times 1 \times 1 \times \tfrac16 \times 1 = \tfrac{1}{36}$, the same as the dog sentence. The table gives no sign which one the text says. Likely and true are different things.

quiz.question: A chatbot ends its answer with "I am completely certain." What does that tell you?

options.text: Nothing about whether the answer is right
That the answer is right, since it says so
options.why: "I am completely certain" is likely text, not a measure of truth.

options.text: That it checked the answer before replying
options.why: Nothing was checked; the words were predicted.

options.text: That the answer is probably wrong
options.why: Confident answers are often right. The words tell you nothing either way.

feedback.correct: Nothing: the phrase is likely text.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how the phrase was written.

explain.text: The phrase is written the same way as the answer: as likely text. A right answer and a wrong one can both end with it.

quiz.question: Which of these is a hallucination?

options.text: A reply that cites a report that does not exist
A reply that says "I do not know"
options.why: Admitting it does not know is the opposite of a hallucination.

options.text: A reply that gets 15% of £200 right
options.why: A right answer is not a hallucination.

options.text: A reply written in a cheerful tone
options.why: Tone is style, not a false statement.

feedback.correct: An invented report, stated fluently, is a hallucination.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A hallucination is a fluent statement nothing supports.

explain.text: A hallucination is a fluent statement that nothing the model saw supports. A report that does not exist, cited as if real, is one.

quiz.question: You will paste parts of a chatbot's reply into a client note. Which part matters most to check first?

options.text: The specific percentage you will quote to the client
The friendly opening sentence
options.why: The greeting states no fact. Check the claims a client will rely on.

options.text: A general remark that prices change over time
options.why: That is general and widely known. The specific figure is the risk.

options.text: Whether the reply is long enough
options.why: Length is not a fact to check.

feedback.correct: The specific figure a client will rely on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which detail could be invented and would matter.

explain.text: A specific figure is easy for a model to invent and costly if wrong in front of a client. Check it against its source first.
